title: 106/04 - Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion Factory Co. Ltd.
text:
KINGDOM OF CAMBODIA 
NATION RELIGION KING 
 
THE ARBITRATION COUNCIL 
 
Case: 106/04 
Date of award: 10 January 2005 
 
 
ARBITRAL AWARD 
(Issued under Article 313 of the Labour Law) 
 
Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion Factory Co. Ltd. 
(Employer party) 
AND 
Khmer Youth Federation of Trade Union (KYFTU) 
(Employee party)

ISSUES IN DISPUTE: 
(In non-conciliation report) 
 
13 non-conciliation issues were forwarded to the Arbitration Council from the Ministry of 
Labour and Vocational Training. 
1- Request the company to reimburse in respect of workers’ health check fees. 
2- Request the company reimburse the workers the money paid in excess of 
the amount required by law to make employment books. 
3- When there is no work, request that the company offer full wages (US$1.73 per 
day). 
4- Wage calculations shall be in compliance with Notification 017. 
5- Request that the company re-compute annual leave, which the company has 
made workers use when there is no work. 
6- Request that the company arrange for a day-care center. 
7- Overtime work shall be on voluntary basis. 
8- Workers request that the company admit those who have worked for more than 
two months as regular workers. 
9- When the company terminates temporary workers, request that the company pay 
according to the Labour Law. 
10- The company must reinstate Chem Sam Ath, the Union President, and Ros 
Phirom, a union committee member. 
11- Request that the company give permission for leave to workers who have urgent 
matters. 
12- Request that the company water the factory roof when it is hot. 
13- When a worker is sick and submits a proper letter from a doctor, request that the 
company maintain their wages. 
 
The parties came to three hearing sessions before the Arbitration Council and 11 of the 
issues were successfully conciliated. Only two issues were not conciliated: 
1. The worker party makes a claim that the company reimburse the workers for their 
health check fees. 
2. The worker party makes a claim that the company reimburse the workers the 
amount of money [paid] for making employment books. 

 
3
JURISDICTION1 OF THE ARBITRATION COUNCIL: 
The Arbitration Council derives its power to make this Award from Section II B2 of Chapter 12 
of the Labour Law (1997); the Prakas on the establishment of the Arbitration Council 338/02; 
the Prakas on the Arbitration Council 099/04; the Arbitration Council Procedural Rules which 
form an Annex to the same Prakas; and the Prakas on the Nomination of Arbitrators 103/04 
and 265/04. 
 
 
An attempt to conciliate the collective dispute which is the subject of this Award was made on 
23 November 2004, as required by Chapter XII Section 2A of the Labour Law. That 
conciliation hearing was unsuccessful. The non-conciliation report dated 23 November 2004 
was submitted to the Secretariat of the Arbitration Council on 6 December 2004. 
COMPOSITION OF THE ARBITRATION PANEL: 
 
Arbitrator chosen by the employer party: 
 
Mr. Ly Tayseng 
Arbitrator chosen by the worker party: 
 
Mr. Liv Sovanna 
Chair arbitrator (chosen by the two arbitrators): 
Mr. Sok Mathoeung 
HEARING AND EVIDENCE: 
Date and place of hearing: 
• Conciliation (in the employer’s absence) on 16 December 2004 at 8:00 a.m.; 
• Conciliation on 23 December 2004 at 8:00 a.m.; 
• Hearing on 27 December 2004 at 8:00 a.m. at the Arbitration Council. 
Witnesses and Experts: N/A 
 
EVIDENCE THAT WAS CONSIDERED BY THE ARBITRATION PANEL IS AS BELOW: 
1- Internal Work Rules of Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion Factory Limited, dated 20 
November 2002; 
2- Certificate of registration of Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion Factory Limited, dated 
15 September 2000; 
3- Annual taxation payment certificate of Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion Factory 
Limited, dated 17 February 2004; 
 
1 Jurisdiction means the power that the Arbitration Council is given by the law in order to resolve labour disputes 
forwarded to the Council. 
2 Articles 309-317 of the Labour Law. 

 
4
4- Letter of notification on the collective labour dispute resolution between Suit Way 
and the Independent Worker Free Trade Union of Suit Way (“IWFTU”), dated 13 
November 2004; 
5- Certificate of registration of IWFTU of Suit Way, dated 26 December 2002; 
6- Certificate of registration of KYFTU of Suit Way, dated 29 December 2004; 
7- Report on collective dispute conciliation between Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion 
Factory Limited, dated 23 November 2004; 
8- Letter of request for extension by the parties to the collective disputes, dated 16 
December 2004; 
9- Letter of request to withdraw the claim from Mr. Ros Phirom and Chem Sam Ath, 
dated 6 December 2004; 
10- Report on the collective dispute conciliation at Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion 
Factory Limited, dated 30 November 2004; and 
11- Application forms for KYFTU membership and request forms for wage deductions 
[for union dues] of workers at Suit Way and Larisaka Fashion Factory Limited, 
dated 30 November 2004. 
 
At the hearing on 27 December 2004, both parties agreed that the award would be binding. 
 
CASE SUMMARY: 
Suit Way Company employs 690 workers and has three unions in the factory. The Khmer 
Youth Federation of Trade Unions demanded that the company resolve 13 issues. The 
Labour Inspectors in Rusey Keo came to help settle the disputes on 23 November 2004, but 
the parties did not [successfully] conciliate [the issues in dispute]. The case was sent to the 
Arbitration Council on 6 December 2004. The Arbitration Council called three hearings. 
However, at the Arbitration Council hearing on 27 December 2004 the union side asked to 
withdraw three issues and therefore the parties conciliated in respect of eight issues. Thus, 
the Arbitration Council commenced a hearing to decide on only the two issues that had failed 
to be conciliated on 27 December 2004. 
 
First issue 
 
1. Workers’ presentation: 
 
The workers claimed that the factory had, so far, required workers to pay for their health 
check before employment. Each worker spent 10,100 riel on the health check. Workers find 
that this is, under the labour law, done at the employer’s costs; therefore, they claim that the 
employer should reimburse this. 

 
5
2. Employer’s presentation: 
 
The employer argued that the company had required workers to pay for their health check 
since this was the company’s policy; especially, before employment, the company required 
that each worker have an identification card, a letter of health check, a family book and that 
[they be] on an undetermined duration contract. These are the company’s requirements. 
Moreover, the law does not state explicitly that the employer must pay for workers’ medical 
check before employment. 
 
Second issue 
 
1. Workers’ presentation: 
 
The worker party argued that the company’s administration has collected 12,000 riel to pay 
to the Ministry of Labour and Vocational Training for their employment books. Learning that 
they are required by law to pay only 2,500 riel for each employment book, [the workers] 
requested that the company reimburse the workers the money paid in excess of the amount 
required by law. 
 
2. Employer’s presentation: 
 
The employer argued that the company would not reimburse the amount as all the money 
was already paid to the Ministry of Labour; besides, the workers had already signed and 
agreed to pay 12,000 riel for the company to have the books made by the Ministry of Labour. 
The employer acknowledged that the cost is only 2,500 riel under law but argued that 
actually, [it is impossible to] have an employment book at this price; workers must 
understand this issue. 
 
Asking all the workers to write to the Ministry of Labour and sign a written petition, the 
employer expressed the willingness to coordinate the workers to demand that the Ministry 
reimburse the excess amount. The amount which they could get back would be given to the 
workers. 
 
FINDINGS OF FACT: 
- 
Having examined the collective dispute conciliation report 
- 
Having listened to the presentation 
- 
Having reviewed all the evidence 
 

 
6
We find that: 
1- 
KYFTU does not have most representative status recognised by the Ministry of 
Labour and Vocational Training although it has registered with the Ministry on 29 
September 2004. 
2- 
At the hearing, the employer did not agree to the workers' demand for the 10,100 
riel back pay for medical check fees and reimbursement for the amount the 
employees have overpaid for employment books. 
3- 
The employer did not object to the facts raised by the employees, that is, that the 
employer collected 12,000 riel from employees for employment books and that 
workers paid 10,100 riel for their medical check fees. Both parties did not object to 
the facts regarding the collections. 
 
REASONS FOR DECISION: 
 
Because the KYFTU of Suit Way does not have most representative status, as set out in 
Article 6 of Prakas 305/01, the Arbitration Council finds that the union can only represent its 
members. The Arbitration Council received the application forms for membership and the 
form for wage deduction [for union dues] from the KYFTU. The Arbitration Council will take 
into account only the application forms filled out before 6 December 2004 – the day when the 
disputes were sent to the Secretariat of the Arbitration Council. Therefore, the Arbitration 
Council finds that this award applies only to the 29 members of the KYFTU who had their 
names on the list annexed to this award. 
 
In this award, the term “workers or union” means KYFTU and the workers who are members 
of the union, as described above. 
 
First issue: 
- Article 247(C) of the Labour Law 1997 states that the employer shall pay his/her employees 
for medical check fees, and that, the Ministry of Labour shall issue a Prakas to determine a) 
the conditions under which pre-employment, re-employment, periodical and special physical 
exams are given; c) the conditions under which the employer is required to establish and 
provide at their expense: [4] the medical exams of workers as stipulated in point a) of this 
article. 
 
Although no new Prakas has been prepared by the Ministry of Labour, the Arbitration Council 
finds that Article 247 of the 1997 Labour Law gives adequate legal basis for a conclusion that 
the employer is obliged to pay the medical check fees of workers upon employment; it is 
obvious in Article 247(c) that when a new Prakas comes into existence the employer shall be 

 
7
required to pay for workers' medical check fees (see the dissenting decision in 60/04 - United 
Art) and [in addition] Joint Prakas 09/94 on Medical Check Fees for Cambodian Nationals 
and Foreigners who are working in Cambodia requires the employer pay employees' medical 
check fees. 
 
In some previous cases, the Arbitration Council has based its decision, at least partly, on 
Joint Prakas 09/94 issued in accordance with the 1992 Labour Law. (The 1992 Law has now 
been repealed by the Labour Law 1997 (see 02/03 - Chou Sing, 21/03 - Loyal Cambodia, 
19/04 - Kbal Koh 2, 53/04 - Kong Hong)). Article 7 of that Prakas states expressly that an 
enterprise or company must pay for employees' medical check fees. However, the Arbitration 
Council had contrasting opinions about the Joint Prakas 09 as to whether or not the Prakas 
is still valid and enforceable (see 60/04 - United Art and the dissenting opinion in the Annex). 
Hence, the Arbitration Council notes, in this case, that Article 247 of the Labour Law 1997 
provides an adequate legal basis [obliging] the employer to pay for employees' medical 
check fees prior to recruitment. 
 
Accordingly, the employer has a legal obligation to pay for their employees' medical check 
fees. In this case, the workers paid for their own medical check fees and then gave the 
invoices to the employer to obtain the results. Making the workers pay for their own medical 
check fees does not exempt the employer from their legal obligation set forth in Article 
247(C) of the Labour Law 1997. 
 
Hence, the Arbitration Council decides that the employer must reimburse the medical check 
fees worth 10,100 riel each to all the workers who have had their health examined and paid 
on their own (see the above explanation regarding KYFTU). 
 
Second issue: 
 
Article 32 of the 1997 Labour Law states, "Every person of Cambodian nationality working as 
a worker for any employer is required to possess an employment card." The employment 
card belongs to the employee and must be retained [by them] in order to get a job. In this 
sense, the Arbitration Council finds that the expenditure related to the employment card is 
the responsibility of the employee. 
 
A letter from MoLVT dated 29 May 1997 sets up the price of employment books as follows: 
application form worth 1500 riel and a stamp worth 1000 riel equals a total of 2500 riel. 
Hence, the employees payment for the employment card must not exceed 2500 riel. 
 

 
8
If the employer deducted extra costs related to the employment book from the workers' 
wages, the Arbitration Council finds that the practice of making wage deductions for these 
amounts is not proper and therefore the employer must refund the difference in cost to the 
workers (see 21/03-Loyal Cambodia). It is a similar case to 48/04-Da Joo, which concerned 
[employment] biographies made by the Ministry of Interior. If the employer had not done 
anything to help, the workers would have had no reason at all to demand the employer 
reimburse the money they had agreed to overpay. In this situation, the workers should be 
claiming this from the official who received the money. 
 
However, the Arbitration Council finds that the employer did pay more than 2,500 riel for the 
employment books. Because it is the workers’ obligation to pay for the employment books, 
the Arbitration Council finds that if the company had not collected the money to facilitate the 
workers in making the employment books, the workers would have had to spend half a day 
or US$0.86 coupled with travel costs of approximately 2,000 riel. Because the company 
collected the money, the workers saved approximately 5,400 riel. The Arbitration Council 
finds that it is unfair if the employer is required to reimburse all of the money it overcharged 
the workers, as it is the employer who loses while the workers still benefit. According to 
Article 34 of Prakas 99/04, the Arbitration Council has the right and power to decide when 
parties pay civil damages or proper and just damages; therefore, the Arbitration Council finds 
that the company shall reimburse 4,100 riel (12,000 riel minus 2,500 riel for the book and 
5,400 riel equals 4,100 riel) to each worker whose money the factory collected for making the 
books. 
 
The Arbitration Council finds that as both disputing parties agree that this Award is binding 
upon them, they may not file an objection or take such actions as lockouts and strikes. 
 
Based on the above facts, legal principles, and evidence, the Arbitration Council makes its 
decision as below: 
 
DECISION: 
1- Suit Way company must pay back 10,100 riel for the medical check cost that was 
paid by all the workers who completed a medical check at their own expense, within 
one month of this Award coming into effect. 
2- Suit Way must pay 4,100 riel – the amount the company overcharged the workers for 
employment books according to the law and the actual costs - within one month of 
this Award coming into effect. 
3- The company must give the payment at the amount and within the time as set out 
above only to the members of KYFTU, as listed in Annex 1 to this Award. 
4- This award comes into effect immediately upon receipt of this Award.
